clue.text: Liberal wearing thicker flannel

indicators.note: one thing wearing another sits inside it, as a body sits inside its clothes

blocks.note: thicker in the sense of plumper
L is the standard abbreviation for Liberal

explanation.surface: A political jibe: a Liberal dressed up in a heavier flannel suit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flannel' looks like cloth to wear, but here it is a verb; the Liberal goes inside the fatter one.
explanation.definitionFit: To flannel is British slang for smooth talking or buttering someone up with insincere praise.

clue.text: Bulk fuel arrangement is critical

indicators.note: an arrangement puts the letters into a new order

blocks.note: bulk as excess body mass
taken as written, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A warning that how bulk fuel is stored or distributed matters enormously.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the second word is rearranged; the first is a plain synonym placed in front.
explanation.definitionFit: A fateful moment is a decisive one with major consequences, just as a critical moment is.

clue.text: Scottish community in denial – loathsome

indicators.note: the answer sits in the following words, spanning the gap between them

blocks.note: the tail of the first word runs into the start of the second

explanation.surface: A town accused of being in denial and generally horrid.
explanation.walkthrough: ALLOA is a small town in Clackmannanshire, central Scotland, near Stirling.
explanation.definitionFit: Alloa is an actual town, so it is an example of a Scottish community rather than a synonym.

clue.text: Prescott uncertain about English (not to be made public)

indicators.note: uncertain letters are not settled in their order, so they get rearranged
about means around, so one piece goes round the other

blocks.note: the surname taken as letters to rearrange
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: John Prescott, Labour's Deputy PM, fumbling his English, in a secret aside.
explanation.walkthrough: John Prescott was famously tongue-tied, which makes 'uncertain about English' read as a jibe; the E slots into his rearranged name.
explanation.definitionFit: Something classified as top secret is the most restricted level of confidential material, never to be disclosed.

clue.text: EU, involved in ding-dong, full of regret

indicators.note: involved means tangled up, so the letters get mixed
in puts one piece inside another

blocks.note: taken as written
ding-dong is the sound of a bell ringing

explanation.surface: The EU, caught up in a row, now sorry about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ding-dong' suggests a quarrel, which suits a Brexit surface, but it is the bell sound.
explanation.definitionFit: Rueing something means regretting it bitterly, so a person rueing is feeling sorrowful remorse.

clue.text: Over-promoted, extremely horny deputy, given a rise, gets out of bed

indicators.note: extremely points to the extremes, the outermost letters of a word
in a down light a rise would flip; here it means turned backwards

blocks.note: first and last letters
the word shortened to its first three letters, a common abbreviation
someone out of bed is up

explanation.surface: A randy deputy, promoted beyond his ability, gets a lift and gets out of bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Given a rise' reads as a pay rise in the surface but tells you to turn the abbreviation round.
explanation.definitionFit: Something hyped up has been talked up excessively in publicity, much like a product or person over-promoted.

clue.text: see 28ac.
Petition against Tory leader – gather up!

indicators.note: a leader is the one in front, so take the opening letter

blocks.note: a petition is a formal plea
its opening letter

explanation.surface: A petition launched against the Conservative leader, with a rallying cry to join in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Against' here just means next to, so the two pieces sit side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: To pleat fabric is to fold and draw it together in regular tucks, a dressmaking way of gathering cloth.

clue.text: Doctor in Kentucky's capital, fit as a half-decent wine

definitions.note: the answer is an adjective describing such a wine

indicators.note: a capital letter is the one at the head of a word

blocks.note: DR is the abbreviation for doctor
taken as written
the opening letter
fit as in capable

explanation.surface: A doctor in Frankfort, Kentucky, pronounced as healthy as a passable bottle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital' tempts you to think of Frankfort, the state capital; it means only the capital letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A wine that is merely half-decent is one you can stomach without complaint, neither great nor bad.

clue.text: Piss around right before Edward acted the dandy

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so one piece wraps the other

blocks.note: a ruder word for urinate swapped for a milder one
R is the abbreviation for right
Ned is a short form of Edward

explanation.surface: A man messes about relieving himself before Edward starts showing off.
explanation.walkthrough: Ned is a familiar pet form of Edward; 'before' places the earlier unit ahead of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Preening is grooming yourself with self-satisfied care, the typical behaviour of a vain fop or dandy.

clue.text: Bulbous thing – pull it out, endlessly

indicators.note: without its end, a word loses its final letter
out as in out of order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the word minus its last letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: An instruction for dealing with some bulbous growth: keep yanking it out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bulbous' looks like an unpleasant description, but it is literal: the answer grows from a bulb.
explanation.definitionFit: A tulip is a spring flower grown from a bulb, making it a playful description of the plant.

clue.text: Former prince allowed Cyclops possesses a Richard Nixon speciality

blocks.note: an ex is a former partner
P is the abbreviation for prince
to let is to allow
the setter speaks of himself: I have, contracted to I've

explanation.surface: A sentence implying the setter shares some trait with an ex-royal and a disgraced president.
explanation.walkthrough: A setter naming themself stands for I or ME; 'possesses' turns that into I'VE. The White House tapes of Nixon were full of '[expletive deleted]'.
explanation.definitionFit: Released transcripts of Nixon's Watergate tapes famously replaced his frequent swearing with the bracketed note 'expletive deleted'.

clue.text: Monk-like, ran after screwing on top of lecturer

indicators.note: screwing twists things round, so the letters are scrambled
the top of a word is its opening letter

blocks.note: the words taken as letters to rearrange
its opening letter

explanation.walkthrough: 'Monk-like' because monks are friars, from Latin frater, brother.
explanation.definitionFit: Fraternal comes from the Latin for brother, and monks or friars are brothers in a religious order.

clue.text: Mark, Barbie's friend, is so toasted?

blocks.note: a toast is drunk 'to' someone
Ken is the boyfriend doll of Barbie

explanation.surface: Someone called Mark, a friend of Barbie, raised a glass in honour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mark' looks like a man's name to go with Ken; it is the definition. Raising a glass, you say 'To Ken!'.
explanation.definitionFit: A token is a sign or symbol of something, the same sense as a mark of esteem or gratitude.

clue.text: US city's electorate reduced by 90% – Republican device

indicators.note: losing nine tenths of a ten-letter word leaves only its first letter

blocks.note: LA, Los Angeles, with its possessive S
ten letters, so a tenth of it is just the first letter
R is the abbreviation for Republican

explanation.surface: Voter suppression in an American city as a Republican stratagem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Device' in the surface means a trick or ploy, but the definition wants a piece of equipment.
explanation.definitionFit: A laser is an optical instrument that produces an intense narrow beam of light, a technological apparatus.

clue.text: Flu best treated without party's lack of confidence

indicators.note: treated means processed or worked on, so the letters are reworked
without in its old sense of outside, so one piece wraps another

a do is a party

explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' looks like 'minus', but it means 'outside', so the rearranged letters surround the party.
explanation.definitionFit: Self-doubt is uncertainty about your own abilities, which is exactly a shortage of confidence in oneself.

clue.text: Hospital corridor trolley's weak screw?

blocks.note: weak as in ill
slang: to bed someone is to have sex with them

explanation.definitionFit: A sickbed is wherever an ill person lies; with wards full, that may be a trolley parked in a corridor.

clue.text: Catch end of willy on fitting – something that lasts more or less 70 years?

definitions.text: something that lasts more or less 70 years?

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter

blocks.note: to cop is to catch
its final letter
fitting as in proper or correct

explanation.surface: A bawdy scene of something catching on a fitting, plus a hint of a long sentence.
explanation.walkthrough: In the UK and US, protection typically runs for the author's life plus 70 years, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Copyright in literary works usually expires seventy years after the creator's death, so its term is roughly that span.

clue.text: What you are: bastard (deny it, twice)

blocks.note: the first word once and the second word twice

explanation.surface: A rude accusation followed by a challenge to deny it, then deny it again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twice' applies only to IT, giving eight letters. 'Bastard' reads as an insult, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Identity is who or what a person is, the set of characteristics that make them themselves.

clue.text: The French president finally in action – removed

its final letter
a deed is an action

clue.text: Crowd before the Nazi paramilitary bunch

clue.text: Put off by garter perversely about to be removed

clue.text: (& 5dn.) "To count, lower your expectations," as Boris said of a certain ministerial has-been (10, 18ac.)
